children: Venu Srinivasan, Shapoor Mistry, Amogh Kaloti, Saurabh Agrawal and Jimmy Tata hold key roles in the ongoing dispute

A dispute over the leadership of Tata Sons and the future of its unlisted structure has brought several individuals beyond Tata Trusts Chairman Noel Tata and Tata Sons Chairman N Chandrasekaran into focus. The Tata Sons board on 17 September approved a five-year extension for Chandrasekaran and decided to proceed with steps towards a public listing, despite Noel Tata voting against both proposals. The decisions are subject to shareholder approval.

Tata Trusts holds about 66 per cent of Tata Sons, while the Shapoorji Pallonji Group owns about 18.4 per cent. The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) rejected Tata Sons’ request to exit the core investment company framework earlier in September, bringing the company closer to a mandatory listing.
The developments have also highlighted the roles of five individuals who could influence the next stages of the dispute.
Venu Srinivasan

Venu Srinivasan, chairman emeritus of TVS Motor Company, is the longest-serving member of the Tata Sons board and one of two Tata Trusts nominees on the board. He supported Chandrasekaran’s continuation, while Noel Tata opposed it, resulting in the two Trust nominees taking different positions on the proposal.

Srinivasan has also been involved in a regulatory matter concerning the Sir Ratan Tata Trust (SRTT), where he is a trustee. A complaint filed by Srinivasan with the Maharashtra Charity Commissioner concerns the number of permanent trustees at SRTT.

The restrictions arising from the regulatory proceedings have affected the functioning of SRTT. The Trust holds about 23.6 per cent of Tata Sons, and the issues surrounding its governance contributed to the adjournment of Tata Sons’ annual general meeting because the required quorum could not be met.
Shapoor Mistry

Shapoor Mistry, chairman of the Shapoorji Pallonji Group, represents Tata Sons’ largest minority shareholder. The SP Group holds about 18.4 per cent of Tata Sons and has supported a public listing of the holding company.

The Mistry family’s relationship with the Tata family dates back several generations. Mistry’s late brother, Cyrus Mistry, served as Tata Sons chairman before being removed in 2016, leading to a prolonged legal dispute.

The SP Group has also sought ways to monetise its Tata Sons holding. A public listing could provide greater liquidity for the stake, while Tata Trusts has separately considered a proposal involving a partial stake sale to the SP Group.
Shapoor Mistry is also related to Noel Tata through marriage, as Noel’s wife Aloo Mistry is his sister.
Amogh Kaloti

Amogh Kaloti, Maharashtra’s Charity Commissioner, oversees charitable trusts registered in the state, including Tata Trusts. His office is examining complaints relating to the governance of Tata trusts.

One of the matters concerns Srinivasan’s complaint regarding the composition of the Sir Ratan Tata Trust. Another complaint was filed by former Tata Trusts trustee Mehli Mistry concerning governance issues and his reappointment.

The regulatory proceedings have implications for the functioning of SRTT, which is a significant shareholder in Tata Sons. Their outcome could affect the ability of Tata Trusts to participate in future shareholder decisions concerning the holding company.
Saurabh Agrawal
Saurabh Agrawal, Tata Sons’ Chief Financial Officer, joined the group in 2017 after working at the Aditya Birla Group. He is also a director on the Tata Sons board.

As CFO, Agrawal is involved in financial matters linked to Tata Sons, including capital requirements, balance-sheet management and the financial implications of a potential listing. Tata Group investments in areas such as semiconductor manufacturing and electronics manufacturing also form part of the broader capital allocation decisions facing the group.

The financial strategy of Tata Sons is one of the issues in the wider disagreement between Noel Tata and Chandrasekaran, with discussions having included the performance and financial discipline of individual group businesses.
Jimmy Tata

Jimmy Tata, Noel Tata’s half-brother, is a trustee of Sir Ratan Tata Trust and two other allied trusts. His position gives him a role within the institutions that collectively control about 66 per cent of Tata Sons.

Jimmy Tata has generally remained away from the group’s corporate affairs and the succession and governance disputes surrounding Tata Sons. His position could nevertheless matter in future decisions taken by the trusts, particularly if divisions among the Trusts’ representatives continue.

The Tata Sons board also includes independent directors whose votes have influenced recent decisions. Harish Manwani, a former Unilever executive, and Anita George, a former World Bank official, supported Chandrasekaran’s five-year extension, according to reports.

The differing positions among Tata Trusts’ representatives have altered the balance of views within Tata Sons. The next stages will depend on shareholder approval, the regulatory proceedings involving Tata Trusts and the steps Tata Sons takes towards complying with the RBI’s listing-related requirements.
